The lifeguards and signs at your beach know today\'s water. Follow them first.
How to spot a rip current
Flat and inviting. Waves break either side of it, not in it.
Churned brown water or foam moving out past the breakers.
A gap in the breaking waves
Where the white water stops, the water is deeper.
A rippled lane running seaward through smooth water.
Don\'t swim against it. Float, keep your head up, raise an arm and shout. If you can swim, go sideways towards the breaking waves, then in.
How to tell if someone is drowning
They can\'t shout or wave. Call to them — no answer means act now.
Head back, mouth at the water
Mouth at the waterline, slipping under and bobbing back up.
Straight up in the water, as if climbing a ladder that isn\'t there.
Out to the sides, pushing down on the water rather than swimming.
Shout for a lifeguard and point. No lifeguard, call 911. Throw them anything that floats, and don\'t swim out without it — they will pull you under. You may have less than a minute.
Closed to everyone, for every water activity.
Stay out. Knee-deep is already too deep to be safe.
Swim near a lifeguard and stay close to shore.
Low hazard. Still swim near a lifeguard, never alone.
Jellyfish or stingrays about. Read the flag flying with it.
No flags does not mean safe. It usually means nobody is watching the water.
Sunscreen, a hat, and shade at midday.
SPF 30 and a shirt. Reapply every two hours.
Bare skin burns in 15 minutes. SPF 50.
Skin burns in minutes. Get out of the sun.
Sand and water bounce it back at you, and cloud barely stops it.
Done today · 1 day in a row
Done today · %1$d days in a row
You are swimming and realise a current is pulling you away from the beach. What do you do?
Stay calm, float, and swim sideways along the beach
Swim straight back towards the sand as hard as you can
Dive down and try to swim under it

A rip is a river heading out, and it is faster than you are. Swimming straight at the beach exhausts you against it. Go sideways until you are out of the pull, then come in — or just float and wave for help.
What does a rip current usually look like from the beach?
A calm, flat gap where the waves aren\'t breaking
Nothing — they are invisible from land
Rips look like the nicest spot to swim: a smooth, calm lane with waves breaking on either side of it. That inviting gap is deeper water heading out.
A single red flag is flying. What does it mean?
High hazard — stay out of the water
Red means high surf, strong currents, or both. Even knee-deep water is too deep to be safe. Two red flags means the water is closed altogether.
What is the purple flag warning you about?
Dangerous marine life, like jellyfish or rays
Purple is for marine life. It flies alongside another flag rather than on its own, so read the other flag for what the water itself is doing.
You get to a beach and there are no flags flying at all. What does that tell you?
Nothing — nobody has assessed the water, so judge it yourself
The water has been checked and it is safe
An empty flag board is not a green flag. It usually means the beach is unpatrolled, so there is no one watching the water and no one watching you.
Sliding your feet along the sand as you wade in
Stamping hard to scare rays away
Swimming in a zigzag over sandy patches
Rays bury themselves in the shallows and sting when stepped on from above. Sliding your feet sends a vibration ahead of you and the ray simply leaves.
A jellyfish has left a burning welt on your arm. What do you rinse it with?
Vinegar, or sea water if you have none
Cold fresh water from a beach shower
Nothing — rub the sand off first
Fresh water and rubbing both set off stingers that had not fired yet, which is why a beach shower makes it worse. Vinegar stops them; sea water at least does no harm.
True or false: urinating on a jellyfish sting helps.
False — it can make the sting worse
True, if you do it straight away
True, but only for man o\' war stings
It is closer to fresh water than to vinegar, so it sets off more stingers. This one is pure television. Vinegar then hot water is the real answer.
What actually takes the pain out of a stingray or jellyfish sting?
Soaking it in hot water for 30 to 90 minutes
An ice pack held on it
Keeping it raised above your heart
Heat breaks the venom down. Water as hot as you can hold a hand in without scalding, about 110–113°F, does more than any painkiller. Cold makes it worse.
You find a Portuguese man o\' war washed up on dry sand. Is it safe to touch?
No — it stings for days after it dies
Yes, once it is out of the water it is harmless
Yes, as long as you only touch the blue float
The stingers fire mechanically, not by decision, so a stranded or shrivelled one is still loaded. Keep children and dogs off it too.
The beach has no lifeguard on duty. What is the single most useful thing you can do?
Don\'t swim alone — go in with someone
Stay in water no deeper than your chest
All three help, but nobody drowning can call for their own help. Someone on the beach who knows you are in the water is the difference between a scare and a statistic.
How close should a small child in the water be to an adult?
Drowning is quiet and fast — usually no splashing and no shouting. Arm\'s reach is the only distance you can act from in time.
You hear thunder while you are on the beach. When is it safe to go back in?
As soon as the rain stops
As soon as you can see blue sky again
Lightning strikes miles from the storm it belongs to, and open water and open sand are the two worst places to be. If you can hear it, you are close enough to be hit.
It rained hard yesterday. What is the usual advice about swimming today?
Stay out for about 72 hours — runoff carries pollution
Go in as normal, rain only affects the sand
Wait an hour for the water to settle
Storm drains empty the streets into the surf. Health advisories in most coastal counties say give it three days, and the water often looks completely normal while it is worst.
How often should sunscreen go back on at the beach?
Every two hours, and after every swim
Once in the morning is enough if it is high SPF
Only when your skin starts to feel hot
No sunscreen lasts a day, and water and towels take most of it off. By the time skin feels hot the burn has already happened — it just hasn\'t shown up yet.
It is overcast and cool. What is the UV doing?
Most of it still gets through — you can burn
Cloud blocks it, so sunscreen can wait
It drops to nothing below about 70°F
Thin cloud lets through most UV, and it has nothing to do with temperature. Some of the worst burns happen on grey, breezy days when nobody feels hot.
You are tired and out of your depth with no help nearby. What is the first thing to do?
Roll onto your back and float to get your breath
Swim as fast as you can for shore
Tread water with your arms above your head
Floating costs almost nothing and buys you the thing panic takes away — breath. Get that back first, then signal, then swim.
What is the recognised way to signal a lifeguard that you need help?
Raise one arm straight up and wave it
Splash as much as you can
One arm straight up, waved side to side, is the signal lifeguards scan for. Splashing looks like play from the tower, which is exactly when it gets missed.
There is a seal pup alone on the sand. What should you do?
Leave it alone and keep well back
Carry it down to the water
Cover it with a wet towel
Mothers leave pups on the beach for hours while they feed. A pup alone is not abandoned, and moving one is both illegal and usually fatal. Call a stranding hotline if it looks injured.
A dolphin comes close to shore while you are swimming. What is the right move?
Keep your distance and let it pass
Swim over for a closer look
Offer it food so it stays around
Feeding or chasing marine mammals is a federal offence, and it teaches them to approach boats and people — which is what gets them killed. Watch from where you are.
You stand on a sea urchin and spines break off in your foot. What should you not do?
Dig them out with a needle
Soak the foot in hot water
Pull out the ones you can grip with tweezers
Digging crushes the spines and leaves fragments deeper in, which is what causes the infections weeks later. Soak, take out what you can grip, and see a doctor for the rest.
Why do lifeguards ask you to swim between the flags?
It is the patch they have judged safest and are watching
It keeps swimmers away from surfers only
It marks where the water is shallowest
The flags get moved through the day as the sandbanks and rips shift. Inside them is the water a professional has looked at this hour and is actively watching.
Trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, chest pain, faintness or confusion. Call too for a sting to the face, neck or torso, a barb still in the body, or bleeding you cannot stop.
Sudden deep pain in the foot or ankle
A ray buried in shallow sand whips its tail when you step on it, leaving a ragged puncture and a pain that climbs for an hour.

string-array.name: sting_ray_do
string-array.item: Get out of the water, sit down, rinse with sea water and let it bleed for a moment.
Soak it in the hottest water you can hold a hand in without scalding, about 110–113°F (43–45°C), for 30 to 90 minutes. Heat breaks the venom down.
Lift out spine fragments you can see and grip. Leave anything deeply embedded where it is.
Get it looked at — ray wounds infect easily and usually need a tetanus shot.

string-array.name: sting_ray_dont
string-array.item: Don\'t pull a barb out of the chest, neck or abdomen. Call 911 and leave it in place.
Don\'t use ice or a tight bandage. Cold makes this pain worse.

resources.string: A burning line or welt where a tentacle brushed you
A sting like a hot whip, then a raised red print of the tentacle. Pieces left on the skin keep firing while they sit there.

string-array.name: sting_jelly_do
string-array.item: Get out of the water and keep the area still. Movement fires more stingers.
Rinse with vinegar for 30 seconds, or sea water if you have none.
Lift tentacles off with tweezers or a card edge, never bare fingers.
Soak in hot water, about 110–113°F (43–45°C), for 20 to 45 minutes, then hydrocortisone cream for the itch.

string-array.name: sting_jelly_dont
string-array.item: Don\'t rinse with fresh water, and don\'t rub with sand or a towel. All three set off stingers.
Urine does not help and can make the sting worse.

resources.string: Blue float on the sand, long threads trailing behind
The blue balloon is the harmless part. The threads behind it run up to 30 feet and go on stinging on dry sand for days.

string-array.name: sting_manowar_do
string-array.item: Get out of the water and pick the threads off with tweezers or a card edge.
Rinse with sea water. Vinegar is still argued over for man o\' war, so sea water is the safe choice.
Soak in hot water, about 110–113°F (43–45°C), for 20 to 45 minutes.
Stay with the person for an hour. Cramps, nausea or trouble breathing mean call 911.

string-array.name: sting_manowar_dont
string-array.item: Don\'t touch one washed up on the beach, however shrivelled. It is still loaded.
Don\'t use fresh water, sand, or a pressure bandage.

resources.string: Brittle spines left in the foot after a step on rock
Sharp pain the instant you stand on one, then dark purple dots where the spines snapped off in the skin.

string-array.name: sting_urchin_do
string-array.item: Soak the foot in hot water, about 110–113°F (43–45°C), for 30 to 90 minutes. It eases the pain and softens the spines.
Pull out spines you can grip with tweezers, one at a time.
See a doctor for spines that are deep, near a joint, or too many to count.

string-array.name: sting_urchin_dont
string-array.item: Don\'t dig with a needle or crush spines under the skin. That leaves fragments deeper in.

resources.string: An itchy rash under your swimsuit, hours after you swam
Pinhead jellyfish larvae trapped under fabric, stinging where the suit presses. The rash shows up four to twenty-four hours later.

string-array.name: sting_sealice_do
string-array.item: Take the swimsuit off before you shower. Showering in it presses the larvae in.
Rinse with sea water or vinegar, then shower and dry off.
Wash and dry the suit on hot. Larvae survive in damp fabric and sting again.
Hydrocortisone cream or an antihistamine for the itch. It settles in two to four days.

string-array.name: sting_sealice_dont
string-array.item: Don\'t scratch. Broken skin infects easily in warm salt water.

resources.string: This is general first aid, not medical advice. If you are unsure, or the person gets worse, call 911 or Poison Help on 1-800-222-1222.
Buried in the sand in knee-deep water, and the reason Southern California lifeguards treat thousands of stings a summer. It stings only when trodden on. Shuffle your feet in and it swims off.
Hundreds of them gather in the warm shallows off La Jolla Shores from June to October. They are three to five feet long, eat crabs and fish eggs, and have never bitten a swimmer there.
Loud, curious and all over the La Jolla bluffs. They are wild animals that bite when crowded, so stay 50 feet back and never get between one and the water.
Pups are left alone on the sand for hours while the mother feeds. A pup on its own has not been abandoned. Keep back, keep dogs away, and tell a lifeguard if it looks hurt.
A big jelly with dark stripes down the bell, pushed in by late-summer swell. The sting burns for an hour or two and rarely needs more than hot water.
Thousands of small blue discs with a clear sail, stranded along the tide line on spring winds. They barely sting skin, but don\'t rub your eyes after handling one.
Silver fish that spawn on the sand itself at night on spring and summer high tides. Watching a run is free; catching them needs a licence and is closed through April and May.
Storm drains flush the streets straight into the surf. County health advisories say stay out of the water for 72 hours after rain, whatever the wildlife is doing.
Blown ashore on east winds from November to May. Blue float, threads up to 30 feet, and it stings just as hard lying on dry sand as it does in the water.
A clear saucer with four pale rings inside it. This is the jelly you can usually swim past — the sting is mild and often goes unnoticed.
Pinhead jellyfish larvae, worst from March to July. You feel nothing in the water, then wake up with an itchy rash exactly where your swimsuit sat.
Flat, sand-coloured and resting in the shallows over sand flats. Shuffle your feet and it will move before you reach it.

Loggerheads nest along these beaches from March to October. Never touch a nest, a marked stake or a hatchling, and keep white lights off the sand at night — they steer hatchlings inland instead of out to sea.

Thousands migrate down this coast each winter and stay close in. Bites are rare and nearly always mistakes: stay out of bait balls with birds diving on them, out of murky water, and off the water at dawn and dusk.
Florida is the lightning capital of the country and summer storms build fast over the water. At the first rumble get off the sand, and wait 30 minutes after the last one before going back.
Resident all year and often within a hundred yards of the beach. It is illegal to feed them or swim towards them, so watch from where you are.
Warm, shallow, gently shelving water is stingray country, and this is the best of it. The shuffle matters more here than anywhere else in this app.
Spring winds strand them in long lines on the Texas sand. Look before you drop a towel, and keep children and dogs away from the blue floats.
Brown seaweed that piles into rafts through spring and summer. It is harmless and full of tiny crabs, but the hydroids growing on it can leave an itchy rash, so don\'t roll around in it.
Slow, grey and often just under the surface in warm shallows and passes. Don\'t touch, feed or follow one — watch and give it the channel.
The rarest sea turtle in the world nests on Texas beaches from April to July. Report a nesting or stranded turtle to the beach patrol rather than going near it.

A bloom of Karenia brevis turns the water rusty, kills fish, and puts a toxin into the sea spray that makes people cough and stings the eyes — worst on the Florida Gulf in late summer and autumn. Dead fish on the sand and a sharp smell mean pick another beach, especially with asthma.
Big, rust-red and shaggy, drifting in from late summer. The sting is sharp and lasts, and broken tentacle pieces in the surf sting on their own.
Smaller and paler than a lion\'s mane, common through the warm months in bays and inlets. Hot water settles the sting.
A living fossil, not a crab, and completely harmless. The pointed tail is a lever for righting itself, not a stinger — if you find one upside down, flip it back by the shell, never by the tail.
Hauls out on these beaches from November through April. Keep 150 feet back, leash the dog, and call a stranding hotline rather than pushing one back into the water.
Smooth dogfish cruise the trough a few yards off the beach all summer. They eat crabs and shellfish and take no interest in swimmers.
Autumn drives bait right up onto the beach and bluefish bite at anything in the froth. If the water is boiling with bait and birds, get out until it moves on.
The water is colder than it looks
The Atlantic here is still in the low 60s°F into June. Cold water takes your strength and your breath faster than you expect, so wade in before you swim out.
Pups are parked on the sand while the mother feeds, and are not abandoned. Picking one up is illegal and usually kills it. Stay 100 yards back and call the stranding network.
Haystack Rock is a nesting colony from April to July. The rock is closed above the barnacle line, and the birds are best watched from the sand at low tide.
The pools around Haystack Rock are a protected Marine Garden. Look, don\'t pry: a sea star pulled off its rock rarely survives, and a stepped-on anemone dies.
Nests overlook the beach and raid the seabird colony most mornings. Watch from below and keep clear of the nest trees.
Both wash up in late summer. The fried-egg jelly is a mild sting; the lion\'s mane is not, and both still sting once they are stranded.
They migrate past in December and January and again from March to June, and a few feed off the headlands all summer. Look for the blow from the viewpoints above the beach.
This coast throws waves far up the beach with no warning and drags logs with them. Never turn your back on the water, never sit on a beach log, and keep off rocks the tide can cut off.
A gold bell trailing long maroon arms, blooming in Monterey Bay in late summer. The sting stays sore for an hour or two, and a broken tentacle in the shallows stings after the jelly has gone.

This is the Red Triangle, and young white sharks spend their summers off the Monterey Bay beaches. They are hunting rays on the sand, not swimmers, and bites stay rare — but stay out of the water around seal haul-outs and at dawn and dusk.
Two tons of animal that can outrun you over sand. They haul out at Año Nuevo, Point Reyes and Piedras Blancas to breed and to moult. Stay 100 feet back and never walk between one and the sea.

Rafts of them float in the kelp from Monterey down to Morro Bay. Getting close drives one off its food and a cornered otter bites hard, so watch from the sand and give a raft a wide berth in the water.
Pupping runs from March to June and the mother leaves the pup on the sand while she feeds. Keep 150 feet back and dogs on the lead — a mother who will not come ashore loses the pup.
Most of these pools sit inside marine protected areas where nothing may be taken. Walk on bare rock, and set back any stone you turn exactly as it lay.
The water does not warm up

Upwelling holds this coast in the low 50s°F through the summer. Cold that deep pulls the breath out of you on the first wave and takes your strength in minutes, which is why everyone in the water is wearing a wetsuit.
A white bell the size of a saucer with long trailing arms, thickest from July to September. The sting burns for an hour and a broken arm in the surf stings on its own.

Blown onto these beaches on winter and spring easterlies. The blue float is the size of a hand and the threads behind it reach further than you would believe, so give a stranded one the whole width of the beach.
Buried on the sand flats and in the sloughs behind the bars, right where people stand. Shuffle your feet through the shallows and it leaves before you reach it.
They follow the mullet run down this coast in spring and autumn and feed in the trough close in. Stay out of water boiling with bait and birds, out of murky water, and off the water at dawn and dusk.
Only in the Lowcountry do bottlenose dolphins drive fish clear out of the water and onto a mud bank. Watch from 50 yards back and stay off the bank: a dolphin that will not strand goes hungry.
These beaches are the north end of the loggerhead\'s nesting range, from May to August. Leave the marked nests alone, fill in any hole you dig, and keep lights off the sand at night.
A firm brown dome the size of a grapefruit, washed up by the thousand in late summer. This is the one you can pick up — the sting barely registers on skin.

The Outer Banks lose more swimmers to rip currents than almost anywhere else in the country: the bars are broken and the water leaving the beach takes the gaps. Swim where a lifeguard is, and if you are pulled out, swim along the beach, not against it.
Thick in the Chesapeake and the coastal bays from July to September, and far thinner on the ocean side. The sting is sharp but short, and hot water settles it.

Schools of hundreds move through the bays and past the beaches all summer, wingtips breaking the surface. They swim rather than bury, and the barb at the base of the tail is for defence, so watch them go by and never corner one.

Delaware Bay holds the biggest spawning run on earth each May, and the shorebirds that feed on the eggs come with it. The animal is harmless and the pointed tail is a lever, not a stinger — turn one back over by the shell.

They look tame on the sand and they are not: they bite and kick every year. The Park Service asks for 40 feet, which is a bus length, and feeding one is both illegal and how it learns to mug people for food.
Both nest straight onto the open sand here, in a scrape you would not see until you stepped on it. Stay outside the roped areas from March to August and keep dogs off that stretch entirely.
The mouth of the Chesapeake is one of the great nurseries for them on this coast. They stay out past the bar eating crabs and rays and are not interested in swimmers.
These beaches are held in place by rock groins and inlet jetties, and water leaving the beach runs out alongside them. Swim a good distance clear of any rock, and never swim through an inlet.

Eight to ten days after a full moon they arrive in numbers on the south-facing shores, Waikiki among them, and the lifeguards post signs. The sting is worse than a man o\' war\'s and can keep hurting for hours.
Strong trades push them onto the windward beaches any time of year. Blue float, long invisible thread, and it stings the same lying on the sand as in the water.

Black needles wedged into every ledge and crack on the reef. The spines are brittle and snap off under the skin, so look before you put a hand or a foot down and wear something on your feet on the reef.
There are only about 1,600 left, and one asleep on the sand is resting, not stranded. Federal law asks for 50 feet, or 150 from a mother with a pup, and that is the whole of what is required of you.

They bask on the sand and graze the reef in plain sight. Stay 10 feet back and never touch one: it is protected under state and federal law, and a turtle that will not haul out loses the rest it came for.

They hunt all night and come into the bays to sleep by day, which is when swimmers find them. It is against federal rules to approach within 50 yards, and a rested pod feeds; a disturbed one does not.
Present around every island all year, and bites stay rare. Stay out of water made brown by rain, away from stream mouths and from anyone fishing, and out at dawn and dusk.

Hawaii\'s shorebreak drops onto dry sand in a foot of water and breaks necks and shoulders every year — more people are hurt by it than by everything on this list put together. Never turn your back on it, and never dive into it head first.

A parasite of ducks and snails burrows into skin in warm shallow water and dies there, leaving itchy red welts an hour later. Towel off hard the moment you come out and rinse, and it mostly does not take hold.

Late summer blooms turn the water the colour of spilled paint and carry a toxin. Water that looks like pea soup or has a scum on it means stay out, and keep dogs out — a dog that drinks it can die the same day.
They crust every rock, pier leg and breakwall in the lakes, and the shells cut like broken glass. Wear something on your feet anywhere you are not on clean sand.
Fewer than a hundred pairs nest on the whole of the Great Lakes, on the open sand at places like Sleeping Bear and Indiana Dunes. Keep outside the fenced areas and keep dogs on the lead near them.
Penny-sized and clear, appearing in warm calm water at the end of summer. It is a real jellyfish and it cannot sting through human skin.

Up to six feet of armoured fish, little changed since the dinosaurs and protected or tightly limited in every lake state. It has no teeth and vacuums the bottom for insects, and seeing one is luck rather than danger.

A wind blowing along the shore sends water racing out beside every pier and breakwall, and that current drowns more people on these lakes than anything in the water does. Swim away from the structures, and stay off them altogether when waves are washing over.
The trades drive them onto the north coast, worst from December to April. The blue float on the sand is still attached to threads you cannot see.
Thimble jellyfish larvae, too small to see, worst in spring and early summer. You feel nothing in the water and come up hours later with a rash exactly where your swimsuit sat.
Black spines a hand long, packed into the reef and under every ledge. They snap off in the skin, so never put a bare foot on the reef.
A mustard-brown crust with pale tips, growing over the reef and on old ropes and wrecks. Brushing it burns for hours and welts the next day, and it looks nothing like the fire it delivers.
They nest on these beaches from March to August, Culebra above all. The nests, the hatchlings and the turtles themselves are protected — watch from a distance and keep lights off the sand.

Endangered, and found in the calm bays and river mouths along this coast. Do not follow, feed or swim towards one; boats are what kill them, so a manatee needs the channel more than you need the photograph.
Standing on coral kills a colony that took decades to grow, and a coral cut goes septic more readily than any other graze. Float over it, and if you must rest, rest on sand.

Winter swell out of the North Atlantic hits this coast hard from December to March, and the water it piles onto the beach leaves through the gaps in the reef as a rip. Swim at a beach with a lifeguard, and if the reef has a channel, that is where the current runs.
No camera app on this device.
You\'re nearest to %1$s. Have your location ready to share.
Have your location ready to share.
Opens your dialler — you place the call
No help location listed for this beach
Share a map pin with someone

No app on this device can handle that.
Nobody has said what the shore here is like underfoot.
Bare feet are fine the whole way down.
Mostly sand. Watch your step at the waterline.
About as much rock as sand. Bring something for your feet.
Shoes needed, and hard going for small children.
Rock the whole way down. Not a barefoot beach, and awkward with a board or a pushchair.
Pick the number whose picture is closest to what is in front of you.
3 — a few rocks on open sand
Optional, and it stays on this phone. It is what lets the next person see whether they would have called it the same number.
Somebody rated the shore here %1$d out of 10 for rock — %2$s.
Look for a clear channel of sand to get in and out of the water.

A washed-up animal shows at the top of this beach\'s alerts for the next two days, so anyone else who opens this beach sees it first. Keep well back from it yourself — a stranded animal is often just resting, and a frightened one bites.
A shark in the water shows at the top of this beach\'s alerts for the next day, so anyone else who opens this beach sees it before they get in.
Optional, and it stays on this phone.

Heads up — washed-up %1$s on the sand at %2$s. Keep at least 150 feet back, keep dogs away, and don\'t push it back into the water; that can kill a healthy animal. Report it to the lifeguards there or your local marine mammal stranding network.
Heads up — shark reported in the water at %1$s. Tell the lifeguards there before anyone gets in.
No app on this device can send that.
Washed-up %1$s reported on the sand here. Keep well back from it.
Keep well back, and keep children back. For a seal, sea lion, dolphin or whale, stay at least 150 feet away — closer than that is an offence under the Marine Mammal Protection Act.
Keep dogs leashed and well away.
Do not touch it, and do not push it back into the water. A jellyfish still stings once it is dead, and an animal resting on shore can be killed by being moved.
